Series::abs¶

Back to Series API Reference

Signature¶

Series::abs() const -> Series

What It Does¶

Returns the elementwise absolute value.

abs() keeps each element’s magnitude and discards its sign. Negative values become positive, positive values stay positive, and zero stays zero. The shape does not change. This is one of the most common unary cleanup transforms when you want “distance from zero” rather than signed direction.

Because abs() is unary, there is no broadcasting question here. Everything is about how the existing values are transformed in place conceptually, while the method itself still returns a fresh Series.

Parameters¶

None.

This is a zero-argument transform on self.

Returns¶

Series A new Series with the same shape as self, where each element has been replaced by its magnitude.

Gradient¶

Away from zero, abs() behaves the way you expect:

  • negative inputs contribute a gradient of -1

  • positive inputs contribute a gradient of 1

That makes abs() a useful example for value-vs-gradient distinction: the forward values are all non-negative, but the backward sensitivity still remembers which side of zero each input came from.

Examples¶

Example 1. Basic elementwise magnitudes on a 2D Series.

auto base = pluss::make_series({
    {-3.0, -2.0, -1.0},
    {0.0, 1.0, 4.0},
});

pluss::series::print(std::cout, base.abs());

Output¶

Series(shape=[2,3], strides=[3,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=
⎡ 3.0000 2.0000 1.0000 ⎤
⎣ 0.0000 1.0000 4.0000 ⎦

Example 2. Integer inputs stay integer when no promotion is needed.

std::cout << pluss::make_series({-3, 0, 7}, pluss::ScalarType::Int32).abs();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=int32, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 0, 7]

Example 3. abs() also works on non-contiguous views; the returned value here is a regular contiguous result.

std::cout << base.transpose(0, 1).abs();

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[3, 0],
  [2, 1],
  [1, 4]]

Example 4. Reverse-mode sensitivity reflects the original sign of each input.

auto x = pluss::make_series({-3.0, -2.0, 4.0});
x.tracks_slope_(true);

auto out = x.abs();
out.sum().reverse();

std::cout << "out=" << out << "\n";
std::cout << "dx=" << x.sensitivity();

Output¶

out=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[3, 2, 4]
dx=pluss::Series(shape=[3], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=3, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, -1, 1]

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • abs() removes sign information from the values. If sign matters later, keep the original Series or compute Series::sign separately.

  • The output shape is unchanged, but a view input can still yield a fresh contiguous result value.

  • Near zero, the value is well-defined, but the “which side of zero” intuition that explains the gradient examples no longer applies as cleanly.

Summary¶

Use abs() when the quantity you care about is magnitude rather than direction. The simplest mental model is “same shape, same dtype family when possible, all values reflected onto the non-negative side.”

See Also¶

  • Series::neg: flips sign instead of discarding it.

  • Series::sign: keeps direction and discards magnitude.

  • Series::sqrt: another unary transform on non-negative values.
